problem: Existing VLM-based ObjNav methods rely on either egocentric local observations or a top-down map, rarely both. Local-only methods get stuck in corners, and map-only methods lose fine object cues.
motivation: Humans watching a robot navigate attend to both the immediate surroundings and the broader spatial layout. Top-down maps carry structural cues, such as room shape and obstacle patterns, that help pick where to explore, while egocentric RGB gives precise object detection. Combining both should improve both success and efficiency in unknown environments.
key_idea: A training-free ObjNav pipeline in which a VLM picks exploration grid blocks on a top-down map (global perception) while a VLM detector plus SAM localizes the goal in egocentric RGB-D (local perception), with local detection taking priority.
insight: Global map-based VQA lets the agent look beyond local views, which reduces getting stuck in corners, and the method uses fewer VLM calls per step, giving 1.2 s/step versus 3.3 s for NavVLM. The goal-refinement ablation shows MobileSAM segmentation and dilation cut occlusion failures by 70% and 'goal in obstacle' failures by 67%. Failure analysis shows that 'not found' due to ineffective exploration guidance is the dominant failure mode, so global guidance quality remains the bottleneck.
method: Local perception: Qwen-VL detects the target in the egocentric RGB image; depth is used to build a point cloud, which is voxelized into a local top-down map merged into the global map, and the detected goal region is projected onto it as a navigation goal.

Goal projection refinement: MobileSAM segments the object inside the Qwen-VL box, the mask is eroded to remove boundary errors, and the projected goal area on the map is dilated (5x5 kernel, 3 iterations) so goals enclosed by obstacles stay reachable.

Global perception: the top-down map is overlaid with the robot pose arrow, its past trajectory and ID-labeled grid blocks. The VLM answers 'To find <target>, which block should you go' and a free cell in that block becomes the short-term goal.

Visited memory and update flag: previously visited positions are stored, and a repeated proposal triggers a 'don't answer number [x]' re-prompt. A new global goal is issued only when the destination is reached, an endurance limit is exceeded, or planning fails.

Path planning: A* on the dilated obstacle map, replanned every 10 steps or when blocked. The path is executed as forward / turn left / turn right primitives with a 15° turn threshold; local goals take priority over global ones.
Termination: stop when the robot reaches the local-perception goal within a manual distance threshold, with a VLM double-check that the target is present. A 500-step cap is the fallback.

setting.observation: egocentric RGB-D with pose (sim) / IMU odometry (real), plus a self-built top-down occupancy map
setting.action_space: low-level: forward 0.5 m, turn left 30°, turn right 30°
setting.simulator: Habitat (HM3D and OVON scenes); real wheeled robot in a lab
setting.privileged: none stated (simulator pose used for the map; the paper notes missing RGB-D data in simulation as a map-quality failure)

numbers.eval_set_note: Per-scene results are reported on a chosen set of scenes; Table 'clip of HyPerNav detailed performance in HM3D' includes 1,000 episodes. The split name is not stated.
numbers.evidence: Table 'Average Performance in HM3D, OVON': Ours, Training-free Yes, HM3D SR 53.4, SPL 35.8

numbers.eval_set_note: The OVON val-unseen split has 3,000 episodes; the detailed table includes 961 episodes. It is unclear whether the averages cover the full split.
numbers.evidence: Table 'Average Performance in HM3D, OVON': Ours, OVON SR 65.4, SPL 43.7

numbers_note: Real-world results (bed: SR 80%, SPL 0.5; umbrella: SR 60%, SPL 0.42; 5 trials each) are in a small lab test and not entered in the numbers list. The HM3D split name and the exact evaluation subset are unclear.
results: HyPerNav gets SR 53.4 / SPL 35.8 on HM3D under a 500-step limit, the best SPL among the compared methods (beating NavVLM 33.5 and VLFM 30.4) and the second-best SR (behind PIRLNav's 64.1, above VLFM's 52.5). On OVON it gets SR 65.4 / SPL 43.7, with no baselines reported. In the real lab it beats frontier exploration on SPL for both bed and umbrella, but SR is lower for umbrella (3/5 vs 4/5).
limitations: The dominant failure mode is 'not found', meaning ineffective VLM exploration guidance. Detection false positives, map-quality errors, planning errors and confusion between similar objects in OVON are further failure causes.
The evaluation is on subsets of scenes and episodes. The ablations are on a single scene, and the real-world test is tiny (5 trials per object, one lab).
The baseline comparison mixes step budgets (VLFM uses about 50k steps), and there are no OVON baselines.
